rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the phrase as meaning that no barren woman had previously borne a child like Yahya.
rows.anchor: لم تلد العواقر مثله، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other interpreters take it to mean that no likeness had previously been made for Yahya.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: لم نجعل له من قبله مثلا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: A further view says no one had borne Yahya’s name before; al-Tabari regards this as the closest interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال غيرهم: بل معناه أنه لم يسمَّ باسمه أحد قبله. وهذا القول الأخير، هو أشبه بتأويلها عند الطبري

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib reads samiyyan as a counterpart who truly deserves God’s name and attributes, not merely someone sharing a name.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب: وقوله تعالى: (هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا) أي نظيرًا له يستحق اسمه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says divine names may be used of people, but their meanings differ when applied to God.
rows.anchor: إذ كان كثير من أسمائه تعالى قد يطلق على غيره، لكن ليس معناه إذا استعمل فيه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suggests al-Raghib alludes to names such as ʿAli, ʿAziz, Raʾuf, and Karim, often used as shortened forms of names beginning with ʿAbd.
rows.anchor: قلت: لعله يسْير بذلك إلى مثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes that early Muslims also used honorifics such as al-ʿAli bi-Allah and al-Zahir bi-amr Allah.
rows.anchor: وجرى السلف على التلقب -: العلى بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author counts twenty-three singular predicates after laysa with the extra bāʾ, against only three without it: 4:94, 11:8, and 13:43.
rows.anchor: ثلاثا وعشرين آية، في مقابل ثلاث آيات فحسب، جاء فيها خبر ليس غير مقترن بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With negative mā followed by kāna, the explicit singular predicate is usually unmarked by bāʾ; the author lists this verse among the examples.
rows.anchor: "ما" الصريح المفرد يأتي غالباً مقترناً بالباء المقول بزيادتها

none: quoted Quranic passages and surah labels only; no explanatory claim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer in the Ibn al-Azraq question exchange glosses athāthan as possessions and raʾyan as drink, adducing a poetic line as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال: الأثاث المتاع، والرئى الشراب. واستشهد بقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Bukhari and al-Tabari report Ibn Abbas’s gloss of athāth as mataʿ, worldly goods.
rows.anchor: تفسير الأثاث في المسألة بالمتاع، أخرجه البخاري في كتاب التفسير عن ابن عباس وأسنده الطبري عنه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says athāth means possessions and has no singular form, though the word can be pluralized.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء في معنى الآية: الأثاث المتاع، لا واحد لهما، وقد يجمعان

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari restricts athāth to household furnishings.
rows.anchor: وخص الأزهري الأثاث بمتاع البيت

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawi’s al-Gharībayn restricts athāth to things worn and spread out.
rows.anchor: وخصه الهروى في (الغريبين) بما يلبس ويفترش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From Quranic usage, the author finds athāth usually denotes abundant household furnishings and rarely abstract things, while mataʿ broadly covers worldly goods.
rows.anchor: الأثاث يستعمل، أكثر ما يستعمل، في متاع البيت بخاصة، ومع ملحظ الوفرة والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author distinguishes seeing through the senses, thought or intellect, and what is seen in dreams; raʾy may be witnessed or imagined.
rows.anchor: بالحاسة، أو الرأى بالفكر والعقل، والرؤيا لما يُرى في المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the gloss ‘drink’ as unsupported by Arabic usage and prefers a visible or imagined scene or appearance; the cited poem is better read this way too.
rows.anchor: فيقرُب أن يكون: مشهداًَ، ومنظرا يُرى بالعين أو يُتخيل على الوهم والظن والفتنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer glosses qāʿ as smooth ground and ṣafṣaf as level ground, supported by a poet’s description of a plain.
rows.anchor: القاع الأملس والصفصف المستوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāʿ is the singular of qiʿān and occurs in this form only once in the Quran; its wāw changes to yāʾ because of the preceding kasra.
rows.anchor: القاع، واحدُ القيعان، وحيدة الصيغة في القرآن. واوية، قلبت ياء قيعان، لكسر ما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Joseph’s story, the king’s dream was true inspiration, not the confused dreams his court thought it was.
rows.anchor: فإذا رؤيا الملك صادقة الإلهام، وليست كما بدت للملأ من قومه أضغاث أحلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dictionaries gloss ānasa as seeing an object or hearing a sound, and istaʾnasa as asking permission.
rows.anchor: في المعاجم، آنس الشيء أبصره، والصوتَ سمعه. واستأنس: استأذن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author argues ānasa is not a neutral synonym for seeing or hearing: it implies finding familiarity or comfort in what is perceived.
rows.anchor: إلا أن تجد فيه أْنساً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Four Quranic uses concern Moses encountering fire, across these passages; the fifth is in the verse about discerning sound judgment in orphans.
rows.anchor: والقرآن قد استعمل الفعل "آنس" خمس مرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn passage about a guarded seat for hearing has a different context from the shihāb qabs Moses sought at the fire.
rows.anchor: وسياق آياتها، في الجن، غير سياق "شهابٍ قبسٍ"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qabs occurs again in this Moses passage, and the Quran also uses the verb iqtabasa for taking light from another’s light.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء "قَبس" مرة أخرى في السياق نفسه بآية طه 10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A qabs is a flame taken from a larger fire; shihāb suggests a bright flare, and al-Raghib defines it as a bright flame from a fire or atmospheric phenomenon.
rows.anchor: ومن معاني القبس في اللغة: شعلة نار تقتبس من معظم النار

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains shihāb as a bright flame from a burning fire or a phenomenon in the sky.
rows.anchor: وقد فسر "الراغب" الشهاب بالشعلة الساطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic usage also calls stars shuhub, a snow-covered mountain shihāb, and a streak of whiteness through blackness a shuhba.
rows.anchor: والشهب في العربية: الدرارى؛ والشهب، بفتحتين: الجبل علاه الثلج

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Kufan readers ʿAsim, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi mark shihāb with tanwin; the others do not, as qabs may be appositional or genitive, both acceptable to al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش في (معاني القرآن: آية النمل 7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author contrasts Moses’s qabs with hostile meteors: in Moses’s story shihāb appears with familiarity, guidance, and light, not a warning or expulsion.
rows.anchor: فوجهت كلمة "بشهاب" معها، إلى غير سياقها الرادع الزاجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the defense that a speaker may alternate between balanced sajʿ and non-sajʿ: uneven paired clauses make the composition disordered, which cannot describe Quranic eloquence.
rows.anchor: متى اضطرب أحد مصراعي الكلام المسجّضع وتفاوت، كان خبطاً. وقد عُلم أن فصاحة القرآن غير مذمومة في الأصل

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani argues that Quranic end sounds resemble rhymed prose but do not make the Quran sajʿ.
rows.anchor: فبَاَنَ بما قلنا أن الحروف التي وقعت في الفواصل متناسبة موقع النظائر التي تقع في الاسجاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Quran merely used sajʿ, the Arabs would not have been perplexed and would have tried to imitate it, since sajʿ was within their ability.
rows.anchor: ولو كان الكلام الذي هو في صورة السجع، منه، لما تحيروا فيه، ولكانت الطباع تدعو إلى المعارضة لأن السجع غير ممتنع عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allowing Quranic sajʿ entails the view of al-Nazzam, ʿAbbad ibn Sulayman, and Hisham al-Quti that its arrangement is not inimitable and opponents were merely diverted from imitation.
rows.anchor: ذهب إليه (النظام، وعباد بن سليمان، وهشام القوطي)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root shatt denotes separation or difference; in context shattā signals difference opposed to concord, while ashtāt signals dispersion opposed to gathering.
rows.anchor: والشتُّ والشتات في اللغة التفرق والاختلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses shattā for diverse plants, divergent human efforts, and hearts that are divided; each context gives the sense of difference.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاختلاف، المقابل للائتلاف، هم ما يعيطه سياقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the two uses of ashtāt, people emerge dispersed for judgment or may eat separately, the opposite of being gathered together.
rows.anchor: على حين يؤذن السياق بمعنى التفرق، المقابل للتجمع، في صيغة أشتات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ins and al-insan share a broad sense opposed to wildness but are not synonyms; each has a distinct nuance.
rows.anchor: يلتقيان في الملحظ العام لدلالة مادتها المشتركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says al-ins invariably appears in contrast with jinn, whose hiddenness marks the unfamiliar and separates humans from hidden beings outside familiar life’s laws.
rows.anchor: لفظ الإنس يأتي في القرآن دائماً مع الجن على وجه التقابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Words from the ṣ-f-w root share the idea of being clear of what clouds them: ṣafāʾ, iṣṭifāʾ, and ṣafwa denote purity, selection, and an untainted essence.
rows.anchor: ومنه جاء الصفو والصفاء لما خلا من شائبة تكدره، والاصطفاء لمن تتخذه صفيا

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says God nullified the disbelievers’ earnings so they could not use them when needed, like rain washing soil from barren rock.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتية: يريد سبحانه أنه محق كسبهم فلم يقدروا عليه حين حاجتهم إليه

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari explains ṣafwān as smooth bare rock or hard sterile ground on which nothing grows.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبرى بعد ذكر اشتقاق الكلمة والصفوان هو الصفا وهى الحجارة الملس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Ibn al-Azraq question exchange, ṣirr is glossed as cold, with a line by al-Nabigha of Dhi Yazan cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: وسأله ابن الأزرق عن قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form ṣarṣar occurs three times as an epithet of the wind that destroyed ʿAd, including the verse about the violent wind.
rows.anchor: ومعها المضاعف، صرصر، ثلاث مرات، صفة للريح التى أهلكت عاداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across Quranic usage, baqā opposes perishing and denotes enduring good and what lasts with God, including the lasting provision promised in 20:131.
rows.anchor: القرآن نقيض النفاد والفناء، فيما يبقى عند الله من عمل صالح، وما عند الله خير وأبقى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses ghābirat in the story of Lot as remaining in God’s punishment, that is, surviving or staying behind.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: غبرتْ في عذاب الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda explains the phrase ‘among the ghābirīn’ as remaining into old age.
rows.anchor: وأبو عيبدة يذهب إلى أن المعنى: من الباقين في الهرم، أي بقيت حتى هرمت

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives the surviving sense of ghābir from the image of dust left behind by someone running.
rows.anchor: ويذهب "الرغب" في المفردات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers deriving ghābir from ghubra as a remainder, like residue in an udder or dust left after a cloud of dust rises.
rows.anchor: وأراه من الغبرة البقية، أوْلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer glosses the phrase as ‘do not grieve’ and then asks whether Arabs used it this way; the discussion is cut off here.
rows.anchor: قال: يقول، لا تحزنوا. قال: وهل كانت العرب تعرف ذلك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s rhetorical inimitability is the majority position among speculative theologians; disagreement concerns whether other aspects of inimitability stand apart from its composition and eloquence.
rows.anchor: ذهب إليه الأكثرون من علماء أهل النظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early works on Quranic inimitability by al-Khattabi, al-Rummani, and al-Baqillani resemble rhetorical studies, despite treating theologians’ views of the miracle.
rows.anchor: فرسائل الخطابي السني، والرماني المعتزلى، والباقلانى الأشعري تأخذ مكانها في المكتبة البلاغية

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani presents his study of composition and rhetoric under the title Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz.
rows.anchor: "الجرجاني" يضع كتابه في النظم والبلاغة

rows.speaker: أبو هلال العسكري
rows.claim: Abu Hilal al-Askari ranks eloquence after knowledge of God because it reveals the Quran’s inimitability.
rows.anchor: أحق العلوم بالتعلم وأولاها بالحفظ، بعد المعرفة بالله جل ثناؤه، علم البلاغة والفصاحة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the sciences of bayān and maʿānī are necessary to grasp the Messenger’s miracle and the subtleties of his proof.
rows.anchor: "الزمخشري" البلاغي، وهو من المعتزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One cannot judge the rhetorical beauty of a text in a language without knowing that language’s expressive resources; Arabic eloquence is needed to recognize Quranic composition.
rows.anchor: فغير متصور أن يكون لمن أعوزته الدراية بأسرار التعبير في لغة ما، أن يقدر روائع نصوصها

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani belittled celebrated poems and speeches, implying that Arabs accepted the Quran’s miracle despite low eloquence; the author rejects that portrayal.
rows.anchor: تورط فيه "الباقلاني" حين تعقب مشهور القصائد والخطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author argues the Arabs of the Prophet’s era were highly eloquent, which enabled them to recognize the Quran’s inimitability.
rows.anchor: أن يكونوا قد بلغوا من علو المستوى في الفصاحة والبلاغة، ما يجعلهم قادرين على إدراك هذا الإعجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author disagrees with al-Jurjani’s reliance on poetry and prose as the place to find Arabic rhetorical secrets; they should also be sought in the Quran, the highest text.
rows.anchor: لكنا نختلف مع الجرحاني، في أن تُلتمس أسرار البيان العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani offers valuable rhetorical observations but no Quran-centered study of rhetorical inimitability; his work is preparatory to that subject.
rows.anchor: قدم ملاحظ دقيقة مما لمحه من أسرار البلاغة العربية، ولم يقدم دراسة قرآنية للإعجاز البلاغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author leaves open what in Quranic composition surpassed Arab eloquence and prevented the Arabs from producing a comparable sura.
rows.anchor: ويظل السؤال قائماً: ما وجه فوت النظم القرآني نظم البلغاء من العرب؟ وماذا بهرهم من أسرار بيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every sura opened by disjointed letters argues for the Quran’s divine origin and rebuts its opponents, while recalling earlier nations that rejected God’s signs and messengers.
rows.anchor: ما من سورة بُدئت بالحروف المقطعة، إلا كان فيها احتجاج للقرآن وتقرير نزوله من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most suras beginning with these letters came when polytheist opposition peaked; the Quran challenged them and their jinn allies to produce a sura, ten suras, or a comparable account, and they failed.
rows.anchor: أكثر السور المبدوءة بالفواتح، نزلت في المرحلة التي بلغ فيها عتو المشركين أقصى المدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disconnected letters are Arabic letters familiar to the audience but meaningless in isolation; placed in the Quran, they disclose an inimitable expressive secret.
rows.anchor: تلك الحروف التي تقرأ مقطعة مفردة أو مركبة، فلا تعطي دلالة ما، لكنها حين تأخذ مكانها في القرآن يتجلى سرها البياني المعجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same bare letters make human speech, reading, and knowledge possible, distinguishing humans from mute animals and enabling their responsibility as stewards on earth.
rows.anchor: ومنها تصاغ الكلمات فيحقق بها الإنسان آية نطقه وبيانه، ويحقق آية القراءة والعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s miraculous eloquence consists of those same letters available in Arabic, yet the Arabs could not compose a sura like it.
rows.anchor: والحروف التي يتألف منها مبذولة لهم في لغتهم التي نزل بها القرآن كتاباً عربياً مبيناً
